title: Not money, fame, pleasure or power (ST I-II.2)
hook: Thomas tests each and none can satisfy

segments.voice: Yesterday, mind and will: the mind sees the good, the will loves and chooses it, and it can't help wanting happiness. Your line was know, then love.

There's a voice that says it: just one more. One more raise, and then the money will feel like enough. One more round of applause, and you'll feel like you matter. One more weekend away, one more title on the door, one more good meal, and then, finally, you'll rest. Then the raise comes, and the bar quietly moves. So where is happiness? Thomas runs something like a lab test. He lines up the usual candidates and checks each one. Today: not money.
screen: `JUST ONE MORE.` → `THE BAR QUIETLY MOVES.` → `THOMAS TESTS THE CANDIDATES.`

segments.voice: Money goes first. It's always for something else: food, a roof, the things it buys. Anything wanted only as a means can't be the end you're looking for. Next, honor and fame. Honor is given because of a good someone already has, so it's a sign of the good, not the good itself. And fame lives in other people's heads, where it can be wrong, and gone by morning. Then power. It can be used well or terribly, and anything that can be used for evil can't be the highest good, which no one could misuse. Then pleasure. Thomas doesn't sneer at it. Pleasure is real, and good, but it follows something good, the way a glow follows a fire. Chase the glow by itself and you lose the fire. Then the big turn. Why does every candidate fail? Not because these things are bad; Thomas calls them goods. They fail because they're limited, and the will is made for the good without limit. Every created good is a part. The will wants the whole. So the hunger outruns everything we feed it. Jesus puts it sharply, in the Douay-Rheims: "For what doth it profit a man, if he gain the whole world, and suffer the loss of his own soul?" And he names the mechanism: "For where thy treasure is, there is thy heart also." Thomas's conclusion: only God can fill it. Tomorrow, what that would look like. Today, just the sorting: good things, real things. Not the thing.
screen: `MONEY IS ALWAYS FOR SOMETHING ELSE.` · `HONOR AND FAME ARE SIGNS.` · `POWER CAN BE MISUSED; PLEASURE FOLLOWS.` · `EACH GOOD IS A PART; THE WILL WANTS THE WHOLE.` · then, large: `WHERE THY TREASURE IS, THERE IS THY HEART.`

segments.voice: Look back over the last few days and name one place your attention kept running: the account balance, the likes, the next treat. Ask Thomas's questions of it: is this for something else, and if I got all of it, would I stop wanting? Don't throw it away; set it down at its proper size, a good thing, not the whole thing, and if you pray, hand that chase to God for a minute.
Not money. Thomas tests money, fame, power and pleasure, and finds each a real good that can't be the whole of happiness. Today's word.
Your line: none of these. Good things, every one, just not the whole. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Catholic teaching, following Thomas, holds that riches, honor, power and pleasure are real goods but cannot by themselves make a person happy, and this sorting appears in retreats, homilies and teaching on the beatitudes.

chat.meaning: Money, fame, power and pleasure are real goods, but limited. The will is made for the good without limit, so for Thomas only God can fill it.

notes: All Aquinas is paraphrased. Check: wealth sought for something else (I-II.2.1); honor as given on account of an excellence (I-II.2.2); glory/fame depends on human knowledge, which can fail (I-II.2.3); power can be used for good or evil (I-II.2.4); pleasure as a proper accident following the good (I-II.2.6); no created good satisfies because the will's object is the universal good (I-II.2.8). The script skips Thomas's tests of bodily goods and goods of the soul for length.
The 'glow following a fire' image is the script's own, not Thomas's wording.
Douay-Rheims wording to confirm: Matthew 16:26 and Matthew 6:21.
The large screen line shortens Matthew 6:21 for display ('WHERE THY TREASURE IS, THERE IS THY HEART'); the voice quotes it in full.
Editor: the hook's inner voice is now framed as 'a voice that says it' rather than telling the listener what they feel.
